author: [AEP] Mendizo
content:
@SW4GN3R, re: your detailed thoughts and input in FR, just wanted to say thank you, as always, for your dedication to the community in sharing your views. This has been and will be a reason many of us continue to trust in the project, for the simple reason that you (and the team) continue to give your heart and soul to the community, even when it's easy not to. For some of us who could go, the Summit was a chance to gauge this in-person as well, and as I've shared before, I walked away from that with the utmost confidence that you guys both talk the talk and walk the walk.

"Slow is smooth, smooth is fast" is very fitting here, IMO; though, I'm not calling the output slow in a literal sense. We want this to be something we're all proud of in the end, and you guys have shown your ability to be strategic on the macro scale. In the micro, there's always going to be discontent here or there with specific things, but keep building to the vision as you have, and we will be there to support.

Once you want to play the "real decentralized game" you will need to set up your Solana Wallet, and then you can migrate all of your assets to that wallet. You can think of it as a CEX account, and then you can move your assets off into a non-custodial wallet. That being said, you will still consume R4s and everything else. It doesn't change what you do, but how you do it. The on-chain mechanics are fully transparent with wallet abstraction.

content: I wouldn't necessarily say competitive. But indeed, they do serve many of the same functions. The future plan is to have player owned space stations at the "in-between" points in space. author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
I was writing a message, but it was getting too long, so I’ll summarize it like this: I also believe that Off the Grid is a temporary game; it lacks uniqueness, and TPS fits more with an MMO genre than a shooting one (for example, Warzone introduced and removed that mode (TPS) within a month).

While it's 'easy' to create a different game mode for each genre, it doesn't mean that the movement and shooting systems at the core will adapt to that game mode. Michael, for instance, mentioned that there isn’t an inventory yet: the inventory for a BR is totally different from an MMORPG inventory, not just in terms of UI but in logic as well! Creating two types would be 'a waste of time.'

I would write more, but then I’d get boring. As I’ve already said, we shouldn’t be "more of the same". It’s crucial to implement game systems that will support the entire infrastructure, and it’s not certain that these systems will adapt to all the genres we’d like to see!

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]

And reading FR I feel like many people don’t realize how a game system works and what you can and what you can’t do once you chose a genre tbh.

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
The fact is that nowadays everyone thinks they are gaming experts and industry critics. It's a phenomenon that started with the mass adoption of gaming and has now spread to everyone.

Every game, more or less, has pros and cons. I don't think OTG is the flagship that will make Web3 mainstream, but it's still a start. As a game, it's not great, but if it starts educating people on how blockchain works, all the better! It doesn't have to be the game of a lifetime; it's a free-to-play, and it's fine if people play it for just two weeks and then drop it, as long as it brings some recognition to the Web3 gaming industry.

author: [AEP] Mendizo
content:
There's a big difference between "all the information is readily available" (from an economy standpoint) and "people actually paying attention". There is a lot of profitability right now, even with everything as "transparent" as it is. As long as human input in involved, there will never be a true efficient market, just because of various participants making decisions one way or another. This is as true in today's equities markets as it is in SA. 

In the long term and at the macro level, things have been very stable for a while now in the SA economy, which means that some people at least are paying attention (and thus chasing some of the market inefficiencies). However, on a day to day basis, there is tons of opportunities for profit. Finding these opportunities takes time, regardless of the size of the portfolio. For example, I have to rejigger my production chain every few days as my local SB situation changes, or as the various margins for components change. I have to constantly be thinking of if I want to do the LP game, or if I want to do the produce-to-sell game. I have to anticipate SB completion to stage materials. This is all labor/time, which is a resource.

I don't think anyone is arguing that right now, for smaller players (and we'd need to really define 'small'), the fees and such can eat into profits. This is most true for micro portfolios (maybe $20-$50 in assets). Everyone, including Michael, has agreed that later updates and loops will help with those players, which we need in the ecosystem. However, the small player topic gets conflated oftentimes with time spent in game, and we should be very clear that from small fish to whales, all participants are having to spend a lot of time in Starbased if they want to maximize profit. It actually is easier for smaller players to maximize market inefficiencies than larger players. So, it comes down to understanding the game mechanics, and doing the research, and putting in time and labor.

author: [AEP] Dmark
content:
I mostly agree with Mendizo's points. There are a lot of profit opportunities in SA, even for smaller players, but they're constantly changing, and you have to adapt to them. I made some great profits early on labs with just a few XXS ships by crafting and reselling golden tickets on the marketplace, but after that, I had to build a larger fleet for mining, and then constantly adjust it to find the right balance between mining and crafting.

Even the big whales face difficulties when the market changes. The larger your fleet, the harder it is to adapt and the more risks you take. For example, whales who held 10k-20k XXS craftsmen at $8-9 each took a big hit when the crew system launched and the price dropped to $3-4 per craftsman. I've always kept my fleet small and flexible, easy to liquidate, and quick to adapt to changes to maximize profits, and I think it's been effective. Plus, I don't have enough money to build a bigger fleet anyway, haha.

author: [AEP] Mendizo
content: I agree with your points, but we really need to focus on bringing in new players. Teaching someone to reach this level of expertise can feel overwhelming at times. You're in a great guild with top-notch resources, but even for you, it likely took time to figure things out. First impressions matter a lot, and if someone starts playing and immediately loses money, they’re likely not going to stick around.  It’s also interesting how we define "small." What do you think the average player would be willing to pay to get into the game right now? Both of you have fleets worth thousands of dollars. The narrative that people are either lazy or not smart enough to play is dangerous. I get that it might feel good to be more experienced or to have bigger fleets, but in my view, SAGE is just a test. I even think it should be shut down once Fleet Command is introduced, and automations should be removed (I can already imagine the backlash).  People talk about Off the Grid and their success—there were no onboarding barriers, and I think they’ve learned some valuable lessons from that approach. While our philosophies on web3 may differ, we still have a lot of room for improvement. That said, I have full confidence that we’ll get the right updates to address these issues in the future.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: The rationale is that we have a sizeable bottleneck in SDU production. While some people might currently be transacting on the marketplace to upgrade SBs, as you noted, those are at very low margin. And my suspicion is that they are doing so to unlock the next tier of upgrades. That quantity of SDUs with any level of profitability will be exhausted sooner than later. So we had a couple of different options to mitigate that SDU bottleneck and make the resource requirements for for SB upgrades more standard:  Reduce SDU requirements -- this risks seeing SBs upgrade significantly more quickly than current rate, which could create a complication in the future should all SBs get upgraded before we release substantial new gameplay loops. And specifically, combat systems that enable the destruction of SBs, Increase the resource requirement rates for all other commodity types -- this would result in similar "dilution" to that which you are referring with respect to SDU deposits, and heavily benefits whales. When looking at our internal data, the largest spikes in LP created comes immediately after a new SB tier unlock, as whales flood their stockpiled components/compounds into that tier., Increase SDU production rates across the map -- this not only makes it better for smaller players (because they'll be able to farm SDUs with fewer movements consuming both fuel and incurring Solana tx's), but allows us to largely maintain the integrity of timelines for current SB upgrades. In the other scenarios, you personally know how rapidly resources fill out for SB upgrades. So it made sense to further incentivize participation in the SDU loop.,

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: This is a super interesting take because it sounds like gameplay has diverged quite significantly depending on the faction.  Oni has no trouble with SDU generation or SDU bottlenecks.  We have too much in fact, Starbases are upgrading too fast and we are literally changing Starbases/components almost daily.  It's unlikely that anyone is buying SDUs solely for the purpose of unlocking Starbase upgrades. I can say that with some confidence because Rome is leading virtually all ONI Starbase initiatives and it doesn't require any SDU purchases. It's likely for the 1-3% margins.  So from an Oni perspective here are my thoughts.  I'm not sure this would speed base upgrades in Oni up, we are still fairly bottlenecked by Mining/components.  We currently have two Starbases open and will likely be open for another 1-2 weeks., I'm actually surprised at your internal data. I'm very doubtful that spikes in LP are coming from whales. If it is... they aren't whaling very good. I thought it was coming from players that cannot maintain consistent upgrades because their fleets aren't big or adaptable enough. e.g. If a player doesn't have the fleets to do Frameworks, they will build power sources while a Starbase is unavailable, and then once it upgrades, they will send all power bases over.  This results in LP something like this...  Day 1 - 0,  Day 2 - 0, Day 3 -0, Day 4 -500 LP.    Its much better instead to have that LP spread across the 4 days.  A whale would be better off doing frameworks for 4 days and then start on PS once an upgrade pops.  But maybe I'm revealing game strategy..., Whales should want consistency above all else, because there is less dilution, and they can afford to operate on the entire map with any component.  Starbase upgrades hurt EVERYONE.  In 99% of scenarios its currently better to slow play and not upgrade so the LP is dolled out slower over time. That being said we are still upgrading because of some future potential benefit that having upgraded Starbases allows.    I'm not convinced that smaller players are the ones taking advantage of the SDU system.  Plus, the more that SDUs are incentivized the more that large players will move over to the system.  And Chris has discussed this extensively so I know there is no easy answer here. e.g. making better gameloops for small players is hard because the larger players will just take them., Appreciate your time and your answers!

So from an Oni perspective here are my thoughts. I'm not sure this would speed base upgrades in Oni up, we are still fairly bottlenecked by Mining/components. We currently have two Starbases open and will likely be open for another 1-2 weeks. , I'm actually surprised at your internal data. I'm very doubtful that spikes in LP are coming from whales. If it is... they aren't whaling very good. I thought it was coming from players that cannot maintain consistent upgrades because their fleets aren't big or adaptable enough. e.g. If a player doesn't have the fleets to do Frameworks, they will build power sources while a Starbase is unavailable, and then once it upgrades, they will send all power bases over. This results in LP something like this... Day 1 - 0, Day 2 - 0, Day 3 -0, Day 4 -500 LP. Its much better instead to have that LP spread across the 4 days. A whale would be better off doing frameworks for 4 days and then start on PS once an upgrade pops. But maybe I'm revealing game strategy... , Whales should want consistency above all else, because there is less dilution, and they can afford to operate on the entire map with any component. Starbase upgrades hurt EVERYONE. In 99% of scenarios its currently better to slow play and not upgrade so the LP is dolled out slower over time. That being said we are still upgrading because of some future potential benefit that having upgraded Starbases allows. I'm not convinced that smaller players are the ones taking advantage of the SDU system. Plus, the more that SDUs are incentivized the more that large players will move over to the system. And Chris has discussed this extensively so I know there is no easy answer here. e.g. making better gameloops for small players is hard because the larger players will just take them. , Appreciate your time and your answers!

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content:
While I respect that there is an SDU bottleneck, I believe it is a smaller factor in why the current gameplay has developed into a single Starbase upgrading process, and that's the upkeep system.
Generally speaking, people, when faced with a nameless system without accountability, or access to information on said contributions, tend to contribute unequally, in both directions, or feel their contributions are unequal.  e.g. Free rider problem,  see Mancur Olson in The Logic of Collective Action, and Garrett Hardin, Tragedy of the Commons.
With the PERCEPTION of inequality, e.g. someone may feel like they are contributing MORE when they actually aren't due to lack of visibility into their own and others players contributions.  This will funnel players into a single Starbased system where the perception of fairness is higher. e.g. Inequity Aversion, Fehr and Schmidt's, A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation

As a result, these dynamics—real and perceived inequality—push players toward a system where contributions seem more equal, such as the focus on upgrading a single Starbase.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: Remember that the gaming community is driven by different logic than real-world systems. Unlike standard/expected behaviors, players in virtual environments don't always follow fixed rules. And when they do,  these are shaped by entertainment, competition, and other RL factors which are not easily captured by academic theory.  There's a disconnect between the PhD's writing research papers for a living and the Gamers fighting for their virtual lives or just the damnation of boredom among the stars of Galia.   Additionally, the structure of the game itself—its fixed rules, developer and design choices—also deeply influences behavior, including emotional responses like greed and rage, where the irrational can become the norm.    You mention some great academic models, and these do provide valuable insights, but I believe that these fall short of explaining the full range of behaviors seen in gaming - especially if that game is pushing or testing the boundary of web3 gameplay.

author: 𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul [ROME]
content: I don't particularly see how you can turn Sage into a heavy "labor market" without making it too tedious.  For example if you made it so asteroids changed their resources on depletion or every hour.... Would anyone be able to continue playing?  Would that be considered fun?  Would the economy instantly become 80% less efficient as players drop off?    Would players adapt and play manually?   I have my doubts. Most would either sell or wait for the next automation, putting us back in our original position.  I'm probably already averaging at least 3-4 hours per day moving fleets around/planning and another 10 hours monitoring. That's enough for me.   On the other hand, would I be happy to play 4+ hours in UE5 hunting down asteroids, doing missions, playing surge etc? Hell yes, ready for that now.

author: Eoganacht | BULK [BULK]
content: Unlimited rental is already a mischaracterization because there isn't unlimited ships.  Currently, if everyone simply rented their ships it would be a lateral movement, assuming renters are as good as owners in their strategy and flying.  However, I have my doubts about that. I would expect a net loss from ships productivity in ships moving from owner -> renter, from skill level, and also from breaking up bigger fleets.  The only potential dilution to income I can see is if the ships left in SAGE v1 and Faction fleet finally moved over to Starbased.  But honestly, it's not really fair to consider this in your income expectations.   Not to mention having more players/ships can naturally generate more activity and thus more sinks/income and more atlas movement.  Renters can only be good for the market.  My concern would when be/if rentals come... what if no one uses them?  Or what if our current players simply gobble them up and we dont get the mass adoption we were hoping for?

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content: It's a good question, I'm curious where you think having whales would cause these issues?  In an open market, anyone can set any price they want. Even if "whales" could "collude" to keep their rental fees high, there's still many smaller players who would simply list for lower and be rented from. There is enough capacity of ships right now that there are always many choices for each playstyle, and owned by enough different people that someone will be there to drive prices lower. For example, the X6 (which I think is a prime ship for rental), has something like 3k holders. That's a lot of different people who will keep driving rental prices lower and lower., Even if we look at "whales" and the potential for "collusion", that is unlikely to happen on a sustained basis. We see it in the MP everyday right now, where large producers are willing to undercut to a significant degree, just to keep things moving. I've personally put in buy and sell orders for 10% above and below current floor price respectively, just so I don't have to sit on some static resources. With rentals, assuming I would find it lucrative enough to do vs the current loops, I'd have no problem undercutting others., The type of ship assets in the game today helps to ensure that there is no one 'must have' path which people can try to 'corner' the market with. With resources, it's not the case. If you need Hydrogen to make something, you need Hydrogen. You can't substitute Iron. With ships, you can use different ships to many different tasks. This makes it much easier for players to find alternate options. Coupled with the first point that there's so many holders of the varying ships, this helps mitigate any monopoly risks., At the end of the day, given what we know now (and there's no point in trying to solve for 5 years from now), restrictions or top-down rules on renting without letting the market attempting to find equilibrium would make it unfair in the first place.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: It's a good question, I'm curious where you think having whales would cause these issues?  In an open market, anyone can set any price they want. Even if "whales" could "collude" to keep their rental fees high, there's still many smaller players who would simply list for lower and be rented from. There is enough capacity of ships right now that there are always many choices for each playstyle, and owned by enough different people that someone will be there to drive prices lower. For example, the X6 (which I think is a prime ship for rental), has something like 3k holders. That's a lot of different people who will keep driving rental prices lower and lower., Even if we look at "whales" and the potential for "collusion", that is unlikely to happen on a sustained basis. We see it in the MP everyday right now, where large producers are willing to undercut to a significant degree, just to keep things moving. I've personally put in buy and sell orders for 10% above and below current floor price respectively, just so I don't have to sit on some static resources. With rentals, assuming I would find it lucrative enough to do vs the current loops, I'd have no problem undercutting others., The type of ship assets in the game today helps to ensure that there is no one 'must have' path which people can try to 'corner' the market with. With resources, it's not the case. If you need Hydrogen to make something, you need Hydrogen. You can't substitute Iron. With ships, you can use different ships to many different tasks. This makes it much easier for players to find alternate options. Coupled with the first point that there's so many holders of the varying ships, this helps mitigate any monopoly risks., At the end of the day, given what we know now (and there's no point in trying to solve for 5 years from now), restrictions or top-down rules on renting without letting the market attempting to find equilibrium would make it unfair in the first place.

author: 𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul [ROME]
content:
HOT TAKE ALERT: WHALES MATTER  

Sometimes it's hard to put yourself in other people's shoes.

That being said, I do feel for the smaller guys.However I'm confident that the team will create new loops and mechanisms that will help them earn more.

And this post certainly isn't a cry for sympathy, but let me offer the "whale side".

Why are we earning the most?

BECAUSE WE ARE THE DEEPER IN THE HOLE THAN ANYONE ELSE.

We are 6 or 7 figures IN THE RED.  That includes me, Bodhi, Mando and several others.

Unless SA goes parabolic this cycle, it will take years to recoup and as confident as I am, there's no guarantees.

No one is rolling in the dough and we've taken massive risks.

And here's another point that SW4G hinted about earlier:

Revenue wise: 1 whale is economically worth THOUSANDS of smaller players.

Nerfing whales could  lead to:
Whales dumping assets,New whales not wanting to come into the ecosystem,
From ATMTA's side, what's easier?  Get a few whales?  Or tens of thousands of players?
As a marketer, I can tell it's easier to get a few key players.

Chris and SW4G have the tough challenge of satisfying both groups and as I said earlier, give them time and I'm sure they will.

"BUT WE WILL NEVER ACHIEVE MASS SUCCESS" is another common comment.

IMO: The MASS success will come from players who want FUN FIRST in UE5.
We have Surge and Racing coming in 426.  Even getting tens of thousands of players in those game modes will be huge and some of them will trickle down into SAGE.

In a perfect world, they SPEND money to have fun.  And we MAKE money by supplying them with what they need.

CUE UP THE BACKLASH...

author: odvb
content:
The thing is, if a game feels too 'pay-to-win,' it can discourage new players and even drive away the regular player base, making it harder for everyone to succeed. And as a long-term investor, you know that a healthy, engaged player base is key to ensuring the game’s sustainability—and ultimately, that’s where everyone, including whales, wins.
The mass success that we all want will come from making the game fun first, just like you said. If the game is enjoyable and fair, players will naturally spend because they love the experience, and whales will still have plenty of opportunities to earn and thrive. In the end, it’s about finding a balance where everyone can grow and benefit, and I’m confident that if we work together, we can achieve that.
Let’s keep pushing forward and supporting the team as they continue to develop loops and mechanisms that benefit everyone, because ultimately, we're all in this together.

author: [AEP] Bodhitree
content: I hear you, and I get where you're coming from. If you take a look at the wallet data with the new tools from Aephia, it’s pretty clear that bigger fleets and larger wallets are consistently getting better rewards than smaller players. When you factor in the somewhat imbalanced LP system, which also tends to favor bigger players, you can see why this creates tension. I don’t have a perfect solution either, but I definitely understand why the frustration is there. As we move forward and the team introduces more game loops and specialization mechanics, I think a lot of these concerns will quiet down naturally. We’re all looking forward to that balance. So, I’m not trying to argue or take sides here—just recognizing where these feelings are coming from.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: Yeah exactly. Took me a while to come to terms with the situation but this is a player owned economy. The game right now is essentially those who want to participate and fight for a piece of the economic pie are doing so right now. I don’t think anyone here bought 1000 small fighters for fun, economic incentive was part of if not all of the reasons.  The guy with the taco stand isn’t going to stand a chance against wal mart. The guy with the taco stand also isn’t going to feed the country and pay all the taxes to fund government.  Sure there is a lower limit on where people will lose money if they don’t have a certain size fleet but there are opportunities for everyone who has a large enough fleet to not lose money to txn costs. Just gotta math it out.   The guy who spends 500 dollars expecting to play to earn isn’t going to make much. For perspective a 100% apy on that is like 40 dollars a month.   The way I see it right now is economic position and posturing and people fighting for the share of the economic pie. Those who can keep up and thrive are doing well and compounding and those who can’t figure it out are struggling. that’s just nature, not everyone is expected to exceed.  In the future I think whales and guilds are the ones who will mainly control the economy and small players will be having most of the fun and it’s up to the team to make that happen and honestly it’s also up to the whales and guilds as well to help make this happen. I imagine it may be difficult for someone with 10,000 ships to operate them all in ue5 and will probably need some help.   Whales and guilds are helping fund development and are taking the risks but so are small players. The reality though is we need these whales and guilds to spend to make the dream come true. Also though if people expect to earn they have to spend. You have to map out all the possibilities until you find what best fits your capabilities. Unless your fleet is too small to earn because of txn fees there are plenty of opportunities right now.  People need to come to terms that right now it’s not so much a game as it is economic warfare. Economy is growing and we have to keep spending and compounding to make it do that. Everyone is fighting for a piece of the pie and the strong will survive and thrive. Even small players can do this once they are above that threshold that txn fees take.

author: Eoganacht | BULK [BULK]
content: HOT TAKE ALERT: WHALES MATTER    Sometimes it's hard to put yourself in other people's shoes.  That being said, I do feel for the smaller guys.   However I'm confident that the team will create new loops and mechanisms that will help them earn more.  And this post certainly isn't a cry for sympathy, but let me offer the "whale side".  Why are we earning the most?  BECAUSE WE ARE THE DEEPER IN THE HOLE THAN ANYONE ELSE.  We are 6 or 7 figures IN THE RED.  That includes me, Bodhi, Mando and several others.  Unless SA goes parabolic this cycle, it will take years to recoup and as confident as I am, there's no guarantees.  No one is rolling in the dough and we've taken massive risks.  And here's another point that SW4G hinted about earlier:  Revenue wise: 1 whale is economically worth THOUSANDS of smaller players.  Nerfing whales could  lead to: Whales dumping assets,New whales not wanting to come into the ecosystem, From ATMTA's side, what's easier?  Get a few whales?  Or tens of thousands of players? As a marketer, I can tell it's easier to get a few key players.  Chris and SW4G have the tough challenge of satisfying both groups and as I said earlier, give them time and I'm sure they will.  "BUT WE WILL NEVER ACHIEVE MASS SUCCESS" is another common comment.  IMO: The MASS success will come from players who want FUN FIRST in UE5.    We have Surge and Racing coming in 426.  Even getting tens of thousands of players in those game modes will be huge and some of them will trickle down into SAGE.  In a perfect world, they SPEND money to have fun.  And we MAKE money by supplying them with what they need.  CUE UP THE BACKLASH...

author: Mandrake [SKR]
content:
This whales and smaller players talk has been around since the beginning of time. What people are looking for is actually the word “EQUALITY” the problem is equality doesn’t exist. It is a myth. It’s better to accept it rather than try to challenge that. 

Some of us witness successful games trying to satisfy every player and ended up in demise. It was already a successful game but people wanted more. The developers bowed and everything went to shit.

The country which has the highest equality is probably “North Korea”. All of us can get together on the weekends and eat tree barks together.

The job of a governance or in this case is also developers is to not satisfy everyone because it cannot be achieved. The job is to give everyone an OPPORTUNITY. And guess what! Unlike the real world. In Star Atlas you can be anything or anyone you want. But unfortunately this world is still linked to the real world which has cost involved. You still need to buy a rig or device to play and participate. That is unavoidable. But you must know this! No matter how small you are today. If you put in the time and effort. One day you will become a whale. That is the beauty of Star Atlas! That is the limitless ability we all are apart of!

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: I’m certainly not faulting whales for doing what they can do. SA made it abundantly clear that each should do all they can to help themselves.   Until opportunities are proportionate to assets held, there is a problem. The idea that whales have more to recoup breaks down a bit when you consider that it’s no more important for someone with 6 figures in assets to see a return (as a percentage of investment) than it is for someone with $100 in assets.  ~20 whales doesn’t make an economy, however if that economy mostly caters to them it is far too volatile.  Market stability comes from consistent interaction from your largest demographic.   We are working within a window of opportunity.  As word spreads that SA is a nearly exclusively a game of whales it will not help us grow.  UE5 are great entry points for small players however that doesn’t necessarily translate to players more deeply engaged in the marketplace. #IMHO

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content: This is not a war and there really shouldn't be sides.  This is about the economy.  Real world models behave the way they do because of human behavior.  The more we emulate what works IRL the more stable the game economy will become.  Right now the model disproportionally rewards larger players in a way that is not sustainable.  No one comes to play a game to be at a significant dissadvantage.  However, If a small amount of assets gives me access to more than 1 game loop and I have the potential to scale "somewhat proportionally" to gain opportunity over time, then that is interesting because it gives hope.  I want what is best for the economy before individual players or small groups of players.  Large and small both matter and bring different things to the economy.  They both have a place. However the incentive for the small player is hamstrung.  And without them, we are fooooked. So we had better sort out a way to make it interesting to them.

@ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics @ROME | Witticus 

Here’s how I would calculate inefficiency for a player. 

This is how I did it for myself.
First you need to make a bunch of assumptions:

They are playing the LP game which is the most complex,
You need to run the math for each component and take an average. There is no such thing as a “perfectly balanced fleet” because each component has different requirements. Some require more mining. Others need more crew. Others need more transport.,
Mining is the foundation. Calculate total possible mining output.,
Then you calculate max crew needed vs what you have. This is most people’s biggest limiter.,
Then you have transport limitations.,
Point is: the spreadsheet calculations for a player with more than 100k in VWAP are hard and they get harder the higher you go. 

Much simpler for a smaller player.

content: Yeah exactly. Took me a while to come to terms with the situation but this is a player owned economy. The game right now is essentially those who want to participate and fight for a piece of the economic pie are doing so right now. I don’t think anyone here bought 1000 small fighters for fun, economic incentive was part of if not all of the reasons.  The guy with the taco stand isn’t going to stand a chance against wal mart. The guy with the taco stand also isn’t going to feed the country and pay all the taxes to fund government.  Sure there is a lower limit on where people will lose money if they don’t have a certain size fleet but there are opportunities for everyone who has a large enough fleet to not lose money to txn costs. The way I see it right now is economic position and posturing and people fighting for the share of the economic pie. Those who can keep up and thrive are doing well and compounding and those who can’t figure it out are struggling. that’s just nature, not everyone is expected to exceed.  In the future I think whales and guilds are the ones who will mainly control the economy and small players will be having most of the fun and it’s up to the team to make that happen and honestly it’s also up to the whales and guilds as well to help make this happen. Economy is growing and we have to keep spending and compounding to make it do that. Everyone is fighting for a piece of the pie and the strong will survive and thrive. Even small players can do this once they are above that threshold that txn fees take.

I want to raise a few questions about the player numbers in SAGE. Despite hearing that it's super easy to get started by mining hydrogen at the CSS, we’re still not seeing new players engage with it. No offense intended to anyone, just trying to figure out how we can boost engagement and get the game moving forward.

author: odvb
content: If we really want new players, it’s about making the barrier to entry not as complicated.  We all like SAGE and the economy, but new players see that it’s 2D, see that it’s incredibly complex with no tutorial and walk away.  Engagement and player numbers will come with a fun and seamless experience. Fleet Command is the actual moment we can get a lot more players into the economy. Because it will be immersive. It will be easier to pick up.  Golden tickets, RFRs and local markets are moreso for the players that have experienced SAGE already and reactivating them with new/fun updates.  SAGE Labs is a test bed for the economy at the end of the day and it’s doing that job very well but we have to have proper expectations for that experience imo.

author: The Man | RomeONI
content: We're very philosophically opposed to the concept of custodial wallets across our ecosystem. For me, largely the ideological standpoint (I want a truly decentralized censorship resistent ecosystem - can't do that if government tells us to confiscate a user's assets), but also from a legal and regulatory standpoint, it's best we do not pursue custodial solutions. Theoretically feasible to do non-custodial program wallets that could manage some functions. But to the extent that is possible, I believe our team would have already been working on the optimal implementations of it. Some interesting stuff coming out from MagicBlock and Sonic though, who were both sponsors on the Naabathon.

author: ROME|King Bryan-Titan Analytics [STAR]
content:
Jesus Christ.  I'm caught up on FR and FR-chat right now.  I personally can't believe the level of entitlement I'm seeing.   Shocking to be frank.
Signal went on a relentless campaign of disinformation against ATMTA and its employees over the last week. It wasn't just one interaction.  Straight facts.   Swagner responded in kind to defend the reputation of ATMTA.

And I'm seeing people lecturing him on how he should respond as a "CEO"?  Like who the hell are you people to tell him how to act?  Sitting behind your computers sipping on your fruit juices and avocado and roast.  Swagner is at the helm of one of the most ambitious space games ever created, in one of the most volatile spaces, ever,  while also building a Metaverse, cyber nation, and espousing the rights of individuals and their individual sovereignty, which is absolutely intertwined and essential to the digital ecosystem.  ATMTA has basically built out a small country. No one has the right to lecture Swagner, straight facts. 

He's out there every fuckin day grinding for this project and every single one of us. The team survived a black swan event under his leadership, and tbh they could have probably given up. Instead Swagner cut his salary and made a lot of hard choices to keep this ship going.

I've not always agreed with the choices he or ATMTA has made and 99% of the time it's because I don't have visibility of the project, because I'm not on the team, I'm not a dev on star atlas, I'm not a game dev expert. I'm just a random dude sitting on his couch acting like I know wtf I'm doing.
So please do us all a favour and get off your porcelain thrones.  Go out and DO something.  If you want this project to succeed, bitching to the CEO and attacking him is the absolute wrong way to do it.  Fucking hell.

@SW4GN3R comments were fully justified and his ability to speak forcefully on an issue without resorting to personal attacks or insults is inspiring. I wish I could have 10% of his skills. In my opinion he isn't on edge, tired, or any of the other random low key insults hurled his way.  He's simply defending the project. And thank god for that. 

P.s. I saw a comment questioning why Swagner was playing OTG.  Ridiculous question. He's a real person and is allowed to play other games.  The irony is laughable too.  "You aren't allowed to be too passionate but you also can't do anything outside of Star Atlas.". Lol.

author: DragonmotherONI
content:
Ok I’m back! Am on duty so gone from food fest, to soccer to getting ready for the next sleepover  so a few things to start: 

Very focused on how we target and thus personalize messaging to different audience cohorts. Women will definitely be one demo group, however it’s about targeting the right group at the right stage and feature set of the game, then match player behaviors based on our features. And that can include women depending on the type of player they are and what features they prefer (ie there are quite a few women gamers who love RPG story and progression based games, also MOBA).
1) Audience and segmentation: definitely going to and planning to spend significant upfront time defining player behaviors and cohorts/segments for both current web3 and expanding reach to broader player types (RTS, 3PS, MMORPG, even some SIM based genre players, sci fi fans etc). This requires agile research work via sensor tower, gamerant player data and qualitative work (also involving this awesome community )

author: DragonmotherONI
content:
2) Women in games and MMORPGS: has actually been growing exponentially- about 35-40% are women depending on the game (like wow). They’re also big in SIM (of course), MOBA and some action RPG (Diablo) and RTS (like Starcraft and Age of Empires) games especially if they offer more story and for the social gaming side of it. In fact I worked on a 4x MMORTS that had about 1/3 women players given the deep story, characters, strategy and co-op nature of the game. They are the majority audience for mobile (also not a surprise). Preference is around collection, strategy, story/lore, progression, social gaming. They in fact purchase more transmogs than guys in games. FPS and 3PS are still mainly male (although there’s a growing female audience with dedicated all women esports teams, but still rare). 

3) Strategy and targeting: to @𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul ‘s point, targeting and messaging matters. Especially when we start looking at user acquisition strategies with ads, SEM, retargeting and more. This is why the above segmenting work I mentioned is so important. It’s not just about traditional gamers, it’s about their behaviors, what they watch, where they are, what cosmetic or feature they care about, genre, the list goes on. Basically it’s a detailed blend of demographic (age, genres, household incomes, region etc) and psychographic / behavioral data. Without doing this you are throwing money in the fire. 

So the way I see women is about what they care about and what and how they play. Just sticking some pink on an ad and going that way is not going to cut it, quite the opposite  also showing a bunch of dudes with big boob anime women to women not going to cut it either. Why? Because they don’t care about that. They care about how you’re addressing what they like, how they game, what they buy. I may get ‘girly’ and buy some unicorn horse transmog for my mount, but I also play Ivy from Soul Calibur and her boobs don’t bother me

author: DragonmotherONI
content: Case in point a recent decision I made for transmog lol

author: DragonmotherONI
content:
So when it comes to Star Atlas will women be our primary audience ? Maybe not. 

However should we still target them based on certain features and how we cater to how they behave, interests, and what they play? Absolutely. For instance I see space station building and customization being a big draw, and how to mod up and skin out ships, explore space, delve into our awesome lore and RPG progression components- basically what I’m going to love too lol. I also love dogfighting and being competitive RTS party time. What’s really going to draw in women like me (and those even more casual), is the massive social component Star Atlas offers. It’s just a matter of how and when we are ready to target them. 

Last topic on discrimination: we 100% should avoid the toxicity we’ve seen in games (Blizzard, Riot, EA, the list goes on), and just focus on the player and celebrating them (and thus our community). It’s not about overcompensating woke action, like (IMO) Disney movies are skewing too much sometimes. It’s about representing the player diversity in interests and backgrounds, and our shared passion in games. That’s what connects us. Don’t mean to get preachy, I just think it’s important to stay focused on the player, always. I did my school thesis on this too lol.
Let’s not be the same old, let’s break the mold and bring MMORTS games to the next level (Red Dead social club on steroids marketplace coupled with a huge social metaverse open world experience), and you get mass audience effect

content: 2) Women in games and MMORPGS: has actually been growing exponentially- about 35-40% are women depending on the game (like wow). They’re also big in SIM (of course), MOBA and some action RPG (Diablo) and RTS (like Starcraft and Age of Empires) games especially if they offer more story and for the social gaming side of it. author: [AEP] Moustacheride
content: Francesca already replied here, but I'd really like to share my point of view if you're up for reading it   I've played some MMORPGs (even though none of them were space-themed), and I’ve met many girls, some even hardcore players (Russians and Koreans are really tough players in general). They aren’t too different from typical male players, or at least not based on my experience. The MMORPG genre seems to be more welcoming to girls compared to other genres, like competitive FPS games.  As I mentioned before, players tend to prefer something iconic to the game, not necessarily tied to price. In Fortnite, for example, some skins from the early battle passes are very rare (or were—I’m not sure anymore since I quit a while back). The battle pass was cheap, but not many players today were playing back then. Taking Diablo as an example, items like the Harlequin Crest or Andariel's Visage from the D2 series added a nostalgic touch when included in D4, and their transmog appearances are unique.  Again, it's not as simple as "girls like this, boys like that"—both tend to prefer something iconic, something that can only be discovered by playing the game. It’s not something you can predict; you can only look back to understand why people valued a specific cosmetic.  One thing that seems universal across games, though, is the desire to flex those super-rare cosmetics

author: ROME | Earther [ROME]
content: 2) Women in games and MMORPGS: has actually been growing exponentially- about 35-40% are women depending on the game (like wow). They’re also big in SIM (of course), MOBA and some action RPG (Diablo) and RTS (like Starcraft and Age of Empires) games especially if they offer more story and for the social gaming side of it. In fact I worked on a 4x MMORTS that had about 1/3 women players given the deep story, characters, strategy and co-op nature of the game. They are the majority audience for mobile (also not a surprise). Preference is around collection, strategy, story/lore, progression, social gaming. They in fact purchase more transmogs than guys in games. FPS and 3PS are still mainly male (although there’s a growing female audience with dedicated all women esports teams, but still rare).   3) Strategy and targeting: to @𝐑𝐎𝐌𝐄 | Virtuwul ‘s point, targeting and messaging matters. Especially when we start looking at user acquisition strategies with ads, SEM, retargeting and more. This is why the above segmenting work I mentioned is so important. It’s not just about traditional gamers, it’s about their behaviors, what they watch, where they are, what cosmetic or feature they care about, genre, the list goes on. Basically it’s a detailed blend of demographic (age, genres, household incomes, region etc) and psychographic / behavioral data. Without doing this you are throwing money in the fire.   So the way I see women is about what they care about and what and how they play. Just sticking some pink on an ad and going that way is not going to cut it, quite the opposite  also showing a bunch of dudes with big boob anime women to women not going to cut it either. Why? Because they don’t care about that. They care about how you’re addressing what they like, how they game, what they buy. I may get ‘girly’ and buy some unicorn horse transmog for my mount, but I also play Ivy from Soul Calibur and her boobs don’t bother me

content:
Hey everyone, want to have a quick chat with you and be clear about something.

We need to be more respectful in these channels. You guys have 24/7 access to our team but the other side of that coin is we’re here answering your questions and reading your comments every single day.

If you want to give feedback, ask a question or just comment on something, we expect you to be respectful when you do it. We should have higher standards for everyone in these channels.

No that does not mean we want to censor you. Give feedback on what you want, say something doesn’t make sense as much as you want. But don’t be jerks about it.

When we go a bit without a game release/update, it gets like this and I understand why. We’re all passionate about Star Atlas and its success. With that passion comes very passionate feelings and conversations.

I ask you to look at the human side of things a bit more. I promise you we’re working as hard as we can to keep pushing this dream forward.

Okay thanks everyone. Have a good rest of your Sunday  @Foundation Rooms @FR.OG @Level 45

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
Im not sure you should merge all together at a single level.
First you need to identify which bonus is additive and which one is multiplicative, then which one applies first.

I cannot explain everything in detail because I have no idea how it has been designed but I think about module/components like this:

Every ship's hull has a default cargo size, let's take a Packlite. Base cargo 5k and every cargo module of size Medium give you 20k additional space. In every other ship this Medium Cargo Module will give 20k additional space, no matter what.

For components, lets say Mining Rigs, the default hull doesnt have a base stat, it all depends on the size of t0 which is still very low. Then you can put some stat on top of that in an ADDITIVE way (+1000% of something near 0 is still near 0). Size and Tier of component will define base stat (maybe Size will be additive bonus and Tier will be multiplicative bonus)
At this point you add a score multiplier based on total crew expertise in mining which is multiplicative (it will be something like 1.05 for example) so the total base value of the fleet will increase more than a simple additive way.

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content: I've been trying to explain this all along.  But it's hard to quantify all the other myriad opportunities that exist given a particular set of very complicated factors against someone's very particular set of circumstances they they are feeling aggrieved of at that moment.  For example... everyone likes to talk about ONI MRZ-19 as being amazing but they have significantly higher warp ranges then MRZ-4 in MUD.   You can use OMs to warp in a single warp to MRZ-9 and MRZ-5 from MRZ-4, where in Oni you HAVE TO buy either an Arc, Bitboat, Sledbarge, or another very expensive ship.  Its a VERY expensive "imbalance" compared to MUD space.  Ustur has 1 warp range nitrogen from MRZ-35 to UST-1 and 2 warp range Silica (with an OM). They can produce FS and sell both Silica and Nitrogen vastly easier then ONI or MUD.  I'm not saying any of one of these opportunties is more or less better then the other, because they all apply to all players at different times, so they may not be relevant.     What I'm trying to point out is that these imbalances exist everywhere, at any time, for all players. There is no true balance imo.  And I won't even go into the fact that re: "market corrects".  Okay, maybe I will.  Perhaps the fact that Oni is "easier" is the reason that Oni LP is 10-20% higher then MUD and Ustur.  Both Mud and Ustur have enjoyed significantly higher Atlas emissions PER point of LP then Oni has.  Is that fair or balanced? Not for Oni.  And that's ultimately OK. (Even though I have claimed about it. )  tld;r   All of these little intricacies exist in every facet for every player at different times, places, and playstyles.  These intricacies breed amazing opportunities.

author: odvb
content:
I think it's crucial to manage our expectations carefully. The tricky part will be ensuring that we don’t set the bar too high or divert too many resources away from the core projects. While it’s clear that we need something engaging for the community, the reality is that there’s stiff competition in both Web2 and Web3 FPS gaming. A side project like Surge might struggle to attract a meaningful player base.
People often mention projects like Off The Grid, but judging by the numbers, it seems that was just a short-lived hype. It’s a weird situation, wanting more content to stay busy but also fearing that such projects could extend timelines for more significant developments.

content: I think it's crucial to manage our expectations carefully. The tricky part will be ensuring that we don’t set the bar too high or divert too many resources away from the core projects. While it’s clear that we need something engaging for the community, the reality is that there’s stiff competition in both Web2 and Web3 FPS gaming. It’s a weird situation, wanting more content to stay busy but also fearing that such projects could extend timelines for more significant developments.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content:
"And it's all a standard data-format, so easy to use in other UE games and make it possible to export for other engines or tools.",
Does this imply that even custom animations and rigging are exported and easily imported to other games utilizing metahuman? Because no AAA studio worth their salt are using off the shelf libraries in their final product (in fairness we have used OTS systems, but as temporary placeholders given the nature of our open development).

"Another use case could be that the assets from other games can only be shown as a collectible item in a display within your hab.",
Which speaks to my comment about incentives. You're either reducing the utility in an alternative product (competitor), at which point, why even integrate it? Or you're adding utility and need to resolve functionality, economics, balance, design, with the existing product. It's more work to make that square peg fit into a round hole than to just build your own thing.

Overall, we're focused on protecting the integrity of our own product given the level of effort and quality that goes into our releases. We have, however, been far more flexible with some representation of SA assets in outside worlds. I do think we eventually get to a point of broad interoperability, but the time to do that is not while we're in our infancy. Again, with the external support being the exception. And those outside teams see upside in representing our assets because they know we have a captive audience. So that's where the economics balance out. But I could certainly see something progressing with Wilder World some time in the future.,
